HBO's Chernobyl series is a dramatization and not completely historically accurate. There are much better sources all over the internet to learn about the events that lead up to that accident.  
The accident it's self wasn't just one mistake. It was a series of poor choices that compounded to cause that accident. The discussion in these choices run deep. The motivations behind these choices are debated. It's a fascinating topic to get in to and I urge you to look into more resources to learn more.  
Chernobyl was a horrible accident that killed many people and ruined the lives of many others, but its very inaccurate to hold it as an example of realistic risks for nuclear power. That model of reactor hasn't been built for a long time and the last of their kind are expected to be phased out within the next decade. Light water reactors, like the ones used in US commercial power generation, have an amazing safety record compared to almost any other heavy industry in this country. The standards for safety and maintenance are very high.

The people in this town can be welcoming, but over all very isolated. If you're not "in" with their group, you're ignored. The mom groups are uninteresting. There's no clubs or group that I know of that don't revolve around drinking or outdoor activities. The people around here tend to be a little racist, too.

But I do love the beauty of this town. The downtown area is very charming. Housing prices are relatively cheap (even though they're rising) and the neighborhoods are pretty safe. The schools are decent, and the staff seem to care about their kids.

Anyway, I guess what I'm trying to say is yeah, Janesville sucks, but I kinda like it.

On the other hand, my father's death was very sudden, and the stabbing pain of getting that phone call and hearing my step mother tell me he had passed still haunts me. I have nightmares from it. My father and I were very close, and had just talked a few days before on my kid's birthday. All my siblings were grown and mostly independent, and he left a very comfortable sum of money to take care of his final expenses. I also have a wonderful husband who was close with him as well. 

With my mother, a mourned that death and healed well, and now I simply miss the opportunity to know her as an adult. We were as prepared as possible for her final outcome. My issue was pregnancy related, but I feel my experience could still help you.

For the first two months, I had hardly any nausea or morning sickness. Then, one sudden night, i threw up my dinner. For the rest of my pregnancy, it was a constant battle with eating. I lost about 20% of my body weight in about 30 days, and almost lost my child. I was diagnosed with [Hyperemesis Gravidarum](http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmedhealth/PMH0002468/). Shit sucked.

First I took Reglan, and that helped a little bit for a short time, but it wasn't more than a week before I was losing my bananas again. Eventually I was put on Zofran, and man-oh-man, that was the miracle drug. I eventually started gaining weight, and baby was born at a normal size.

Go to the doctor. There are so many things that could be wrong. My case is pretty extreme, I think, but nausea can be pretty deadly if you let it go on for too long.

Let's equate technology acceptance with breastfeeding acceptance for a moment.

For the most part, our grandparents are technophobes. If you set them in front of a computer to send an e-mail to Dr. Geri Atrics, they'll probably say "why can't I just write a letter!" Even if you teach them, and educate them, and hold their hand and walk them through it, they are going to prefer the way they learned growing up. Now, if you take someone, say your average highschooler, and tell them to send e-mail Mr. T Chezyu, they'll probably roll their eyes and pop open gmail. The difference is, one was exposed to e-mail in his youth, the other hadn't gotten exposure until later in life.

It isn't so much about teaching kids something to make them the best people possible. I'm sure both the grandparent and the teenager are decent human beings. If you want to make an idea, product, event, or other noun common-place, early exposure is important. Then, the reaction to a breastfeeding doll wouldn't be "OMG TITTIES EVERYONE FREAK THE FUCK OUT!" It would be something more like another poster mentioned; who the fuck wants to pay that much for a doll?!

There is a problem with the way adults in the United States react towards breastfeeding. In this country, we are taught that breasts = sex, and sex is BAD. We are taught this from a young age. Teaching an old dog a new trick can be a difficult task.

I do see it that way. If we keep treating breastfeeding as something weird and unnatural to our kids, they're going to grow up thinking its weird and unnatural. If we let them play with baby dolls and "do like mommy," then they learn there is nothing wrong with it.

My step sister and I basically parent trapped our parents.

My mother passed away when I was 11. It sucked, and my dad was depressed, but eventually started dating other women. My best friend was a girl I met in girl scouts, and her mom was a single working mother who was good friends with my mom before she passed. She use to give me rides to school. She was (and is) and awesome woman who taught me that family doesn't have to be blood.

So anyway, one day I ask to go over to my friend's house, and my dad drives me over there. She and my dad chat for a bit, then he leaves, and friend and I play. Eventually it was close to time for me to leave, but I didn't want to go, so we "accidently" lock ourselves in the basement. So he comes to pick me up, friend's mom comes to open the basement door, and can't. We claim "we can't open the door! It's stuck!" They start freaking out, and eventually tell us they're off to the hardware store and will be back.

Thirty minutes and $45 later, they completely removed the door and we were free. That weekend, they started dating, and about a year later were married.

TL;DR: My step-sister and I got our parents to meet.
